tier2.text: The pineal body releases melatonin, a hormone that causes drowsiness and is important in regulating the sleep-wake cycle. Also called the pineal gland, the pineal body is a small cone-shaped structure that extends backward from the third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity in the brain. Besides parts of nerve cells and supporting cells called neuroglia, the gland holds specialized secreting cells called pinealocytes. Pinealocytes make melatonin and release it straight into the cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid around the brain and spinal cord, and this fluid carries the melatonin into the blood. When light reaches the eyes, a nerve signal travels to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, a region in the brain's hypothalamus that helps regulate biological rhythms. The signal then passes to the spinal cord and on to the pineal body, where melatonin production slows; as blood levels of melatonin fall, a person becomes more wakeful. In contrast, as light fades in the evening, melatonin production rises, and the higher blood levels cause drowsiness. Melatonin may also influence circadian rhythms, the body’s ups and downs with dark and light; these rhythms affect sleepiness and wakefulness as well as appetite and body temperature. Children have higher melatonin levels than adults, which may delay puberty by blocking the release of certain hormones from the pituitary gland, a bean-sized organ that secretes hormones.
